**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Internal — for discussion at Thursday's planning session

Over the past few weeks we've been circling a question that keeps coming up in standups and side conversations: our inference and fine-tuning workloads are bumping against the ceiling of the hardware we own, and we need to decide whether the right response is to purchase additional local capacity or to invest in squeezing more out of what we already have. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about the trade-off, because I don't believe it's as close a call as our recent conversations have suggested — though I want to be honest about where my confidence is soft.

The case for buying more hardware is the obvious one. It's fast, at least in the sense that a purchase order is faster than a quarter of careful engineering work, and it removes the constraint entirely rather than managing it. If our growth curve is real, we will need more absolute capacity eventually, and there's an argument that we're simply delaying the inevitable. There's also a genuine opportunity cost to under-capacity: every time a fine-tuning run gets queued behind someone else's batch job, or an experiment gets shelved because there's no GPU free, we're implicitly trading away work we might have shipped. That cost is real, it's recurring, and it doesn't show up on any invoice, which makes it easy to underestimate.

But when I look at our actual utilisation numbers, I don't think the constraint is capacity. It's scheduling. Our fleet sits idle a substantial fraction of the time — overnight, between batch jobs, during the long tail of inference traffic — and when it is busy, it's often busy on work that doesn't need to be busy right then. We run models at batch sizes tuned months ago for workloads that have since changed. We keep warm replicas for services that see a handful of requests a day. We have no meaningful priority system, so a low-stakes internal experiment can crowd out a customer-facing job. In other words, we're proposing to buy our way out of a problem that is substantially of our own making, and buying hardware before fixing that is like buying a second car because the first one is always parked in the wrong place.

The economics reinforce this. Hardware purchases are lumpy, front-loaded, and largely irreversible at our scale — once we've bought accelerators, they depreciate whether we use them or not, and reselling them recovers only a fraction of cost in a market that moves fast. Improving utilisation, by contrast, is mostly an investment of engineering time, which is the resource we already have and are already spending. It's also reversible in the way capital expenditure is not: if we build better scheduling and batching and it turns out we were wrong about our headroom, we've lost a few sprints, not a capital budget. And the work itself compounds — better queueing, dynamic batching, and honest capacity telemetry make us more efficient with whatever hardware we own, including anything we buy later. The same cannot be said of the reverse ordering.

On latency, I want to be careful, because this is where the utilisation argument is weakest. If we push utilisation higher through aggressive batching and queueing, tail latency for interactive inference will get worse before it gets better; that's the classic trade-off, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. My view is that we can accept some of that degradation for internal workloads, and that for the customer-facing paths we should carve out explicit latency-sensitive capacity rather than letting the scheduler treat everything as fungible. That carve-out is itself part of the utilisation work, not a reason to abandon it.

On reliability, buying more hardware does buy something real: headroom means a failed node doesn't immediately mean degraded service. But we can get most of that benefit more cheaply by holding a deliberate utilisation buffer — running the fleet at a target that leaves room for failure — rather than by adding nodes we don't yet know how to keep busy.

So my recommendation is this: we defer the purchase for one quarter, and in that time we do the unglamorous work — real telemetry, a proper scheduler with priorities, dynamic batching on the hot paths, and an honest audit of what's running and why. We set a concrete trigger now: if, at the end of that quarter, sustained utilisation on the improved fleet exceeds a threshold we agree on in advance, we go straight to procurement with the team's full support, and the utilisation work will have made that purchase cheaper and better-targeted rather than merely delayed.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. My read of our utilisation data could be wrong; idle time on paper doesn't always translate into recoverable capacity, and there may be structural reasons — memory fragmentation, model residency requirements, thermal constraints — that make our theoretical headroom harder to realise than the dashboards suggest. If that turns out to be true, we'll have spent a quarter learning it, and we'll buy with better information. That's a cost I'm willing to accept, and I'd rather take it than the alternative: spending capital now to paper over a scheduling problem we'd still own afterward.

Happy to debate the trigger threshold and the sequencing at Thursday's session.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure working group
**Re:** Recommendation on Q3 compute capacity decision

**Summary**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of our existing hardware before committing to any new purchases. The case is not that we will never need more capacity — we likely will — but that the cheapest, most reversible, and most informative next step is to treat our current fleet as if it were already the larger fleet we're asking to buy.

**The situation**

Our inference and fine-tuning workloads currently run on a small pool of local accelerators. Peak demand now exceeds peak capacity, and we've started queueing jobs, which has surfaced as a real friction point: researchers wait hours for GPU time, and at least one project has quietly deprioritised an experiment because of it. The obvious response is to buy more cards. The less obvious response is to ask why a fleet that averages well under half utilisation by our own telemetry feels perpetually short.

**Cost**

The purchase price of new hardware is only the visible part. Add power, cooling, rack space, the ops burden of managing a larger fleet, and — most importantly for a team our size — the depreciation risk. Accelerator generations turn over quickly, and hardware bought today at a premium may be worth a fraction of that in eighteen months. By contrast, the utilisation work is mostly engineering time we'd spend anyway: better job scheduling, a shared queue with priorities, checkpointing so long jobs can be preempted, and honest instrumentation of who is using what. Even a generous estimate of that effort is an order of magnitude cheaper than the capital outlay, and it pays off regardless of what we eventually buy.

**Latency**

There is a genuine latency argument for more hardware: interactive development — notebook experimentation, quick fine-tuning runs, debugging — suffers when the queue is deep. This is the strongest point in favour of buying, and we take it seriously. But it's worth noting that most of our latency pain is not raw compute throughput; it's scheduling latency, the gap between "I want a GPU" and "I have a GPU." A proper queue with fair sharing and preemption attacks that directly. If, after that, interactive jobs still wait too long, we'll know precisely how much capacity we're missing and can buy exactly that, rather than guessing.

**Reliability**

A larger fleet is not automatically a more reliable one. More hardware means more failure modes, more driver and firmware drift, and more surface area for the kind of silent degradation that eats a weekend. Our current fleet has had two outages this quarter, both traceable to configuration drift rather than capacity. Utilisation work forces us to build the operational discipline — monitoring, health checks, graceful drain and failover — that we would need anyway before scaling. Buying capacity before we have that discipline would multiply our existing problems, not dilute them.

**Opportunity cost**

Every dollar and every engineer-hour spent on procurement and fleet expansion is a dollar and an hour not spent on the product work that actually differentiates us. The reverse is also true, of course: time spent on scheduling infrastructure is time not spent shipping features. But the utilisation path is bounded — we estimate four to six weeks of focused effort — whereas hardware ownership is an open-ended commitment. There's also a subtler opportunity cost: if we buy now and utilisation stays low, we'll have purchased a permanent reminder that we solved a scheduling problem with capital.

**Reversibility**

This is the decisive factor for us. Hardware purchases are largely irreversible at our scale; resale markets for used accelerators are thin, and the money doesn't come back. Utilisation improvements are almost entirely reversible — if a scheduling change proves worse than the status quo, we roll it back in an afternoon. When two options are plausibly similar in benefit, the reversible one is worth more, because it preserves our ability to learn before we lock in.

**Uncertainty and what would change our mind**

We want to be honest about the limits of this analysis. Our utilisation telemetry is imperfect and may undercount real contention; if a proper audit shows the fleet is genuinely saturated at 80% or above, the buy case strengthens considerably. Demand forecasts are also uncertain — if we land a project requiring sustained dedicated capacity, queuing optimisations won't conjure silicon that doesn't exist. We propose a concrete tripwire: if, after the utilisation quarter, p95 queue wait for interactive jobs still exceeds our agreed threshold, we proceed immediately to procurement with a much better-grounded sizing estimate.

**Recommendation**

Fund a focused, time-boxed utilisation effort now. Revisit procurement at the end of the quarter with real data in hand. We'll spend less, learn more, and keep the option to buy — with confidence rather than urgency — if the numbers say we should.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure working group
**Re:** Recommendation on our local inference capacity

**Summary**

We are at the point where our local GPU fleet is saturated during peak hours, and the question on the table is whether to purchase additional hardware or invest in raising the utilisation of what we already own. After several weeks of measurement and modelling, our recommendation is to spend the next quarter on utilisation work first, and hold the capital purchase as a contingent decision we can make quickly if that work falls short. The reasoning below is not a case against buying hardware; it is a case about sequencing.

**Where we actually are**

Our fleet runs at roughly 55% average utilisation across the week, but that number hides the real problem: peak-hour utilisation sits above 90% on three of our eight nodes, while the remainder idle much of the day. The bottleneck is not aggregate capacity but scheduling and workload placement. Batch jobs queue behind latency-sensitive inference, models are pinned to nodes for historical rather than technical reasons, and our autoscaling only reacts to per-node load rather than queue depth. In other words, we are experiencing a scheduling failure that looks, from the outside, like a capacity shortage.

**The case for buying now**

Buying hardware has real appeal. It is simple, it is fast to reason about, and it removes the problem categorically rather than incrementally. Lead times are currently four to six weeks, and prices on the class of card we want have been stable. If our workload grows the way the product team projects, we will need more absolute capacity within two quarters regardless of how well we schedule. There is also an argument that engineering time spent on scheduler work is time not spent on product features, and that the "free" option of better utilisation is not free at all.

**The case for utilisation first**

The strongest argument for the utilisation path is reversibility. Capital spent on GPUs is spent; if demand shifts, if a hosted API becomes materially cheaper, or if the next hardware generation makes our purchase look premature, we own depreciating inventory and the opportunity cost of the cash. The utilisation work, by contrast, is mostly engineering time we would spend anyway on operational hygiene, and its outputs — better queueing, dynamic model placement, batch-aware routing — remain valuable even after we do eventually buy more hardware. Nothing about improving scheduling is wasted.

The cost asymmetry also matters. A meaningful capacity addition is a five-figure capital outlay plus ongoing power, cooling, and rack space, and it carries a maintenance tail we have historically underestimated. The utilisation work is perhaps six weeks of one engineer's time, concentrated. If it recovers even half of the idle capacity implied by our peak-versus-average gap, we buy ourselves a quarter or more of headroom at a fraction of the cost, and we make the eventual purchase better-informed: we will know our true steady-state demand rather than our demand-under-current-inefficiency.

Latency is the one place where the hardware option wins outright. More nodes means more headroom for bursty traffic and less queue-induced tail latency. Squeezing utilisation higher tends to raise p99 latency even as it raises throughput, and we should be honest that a well-packed cluster is a more fragile one. Our mitigation is to treat 80% sustained utilisation as a hard ceiling in our planning, not a target, and to keep burst capacity in reserve. Reliability cuts both ways: more nodes give us redundancy, but our current failure mode is not hardware loss — it is queue collapse during peaks, which better scheduling addresses directly.

**Recommendation**

Fund a focused six-week utilisation effort: dynamic model placement, queue-depth-based routing, and off-peak batching of non-urgent work. Set explicit success criteria now — if peak-hour p95 latency stays within our SLO at 80% utilisation, we defer purchase by one quarter; if not, we trigger the hardware order immediately with pre-approved budget so we lose no time to deliberation. This keeps the decision reversible, avoids paying capital prices for a scheduling problem, and positions us to buy with better information if buying is genuinely needed.

**Uncertainty**

The main risk is that we underestimate demand growth and end up buying later under time pressure, at worse prices or with worse lead times. The pre-approved contingency order is our hedge against that. The second risk is that utilisation work proves harder than estimated; we will checkpoint at week three and escalate if progress is off track.

We're happy to walk through the utilisation data with anyone who wants the detail.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Thursday

We've reached the point in the quarter where the queue for our inference cluster has become visible enough that people are asking what we're going to do about it. The honest framing of the question is not "do we need more compute?" — we clearly do, at peak — but rather "is buying more hardware the cheapest and most reversible way to get it?" I want to walk through how I'm thinking about that, because I've changed my own mind twice in the past two weeks.

The case for buying is straightforward. Our p95 latency on the shared cluster has crept from about 400ms to over a second during business hours, and latency is not an abstract metric here: it shows up as abandoned batch jobs, as researchers serialising work they used to parallelise, and as a quiet tax on every experiment anyone runs. When a tool gets slow, people stop using it, and then we learn less. There's also a reliability argument. We currently run with essentially no headroom, which means a single node failure during a heavy window degrades service for everyone rather than for a subset. That's a fragile way to operate, and fragility has a way of converting into an outage at the worst possible moment.

But the case for buying rests on an assumption I don't think we've tested: that our hardware is actually well used. The utilisation dashboards tell a murkier story than the queue does. Average GPU occupancy across the fleet sits somewhere in the low forties, which is not obviously a capacity problem — it's a scheduling problem. A meaningful share of our allocation is held by long-running notebook sessions that are idle most of the day, and our batch queue is FIFO, which means a two-minute job can wait behind a six-hour one. We also have no meaningful preemption, so people over-request memory "just in case," and that reservation is then unavailable to everyone else even while the GPU itself sits mostly dark. If we fixed even half of this, we would effectively manufacture capacity without spending anything.

The cost comparison makes the case for trying that first quite strongly. A modest hardware purchase — two more nodes — is roughly a year of an engineer's fully-loaded cost, plus the ongoing burden of power, cooling, and someone's attention when a driver update goes sideways. The alternative is a few weeks of focused work: a fairer scheduler, aggressive idle-timeout reclamation, memory over-request limits, and better telemetry so we can actually see who is using what. That work is not glamorous, but it is cheap, and unlike hardware it compounds — the scheduling discipline we build now is exactly what we'll need when the fleet is twice this size.

There's also the opportunity cost to weigh, and it cuts both ways, which is worth being honest about. Every week engineers spend on scheduler work is a week not spent on the product roadmap. But every dollar spent on hardware that sits at fifty percent occupancy is a dollar not spent on anything else, forever, and hardware also carries a hidden second cost: it commits us. Once the purchase is made and racked, the organisation's instinct is to keep filling it, and utilisation discipline quietly becomes someone else's problem. Buying capacity before fixing utilisation tends to lock in the bad habits that created the shortage.

Reversibility is the tiebreaker for me. Software changes can be undone; a purchase order mostly can't. If we spend six weeks on utilisation work and it fails — if it turns out the queue is genuinely driven by real, dense demand rather than scheduling artefacts — we will have lost six weeks and gained a much better empirical case for the purchase, which we can then make to finance with data instead of vibes. If we buy first and it turns out we didn't need to, we've spent capital we can't recover and we still don't understand our own workload.

So my recommendation is: do the utilisation work first, with a hard time-box of six weeks and a pre-agreed trigger. If, at the end of that window, sustained p95 latency during business hours still exceeds 800ms with utilisation above 75%, we submit the hardware request immediately and without relitigating the decision. That gives us a real commitment device rather than an indefinite deferral, which I know is the legitimate worry on the other side of this argument — that "measure twice" becomes an excuse never to cut.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. My read of the dashboards could be wrong; idle notebook sessions may matter less than they appear, and peak demand may be growing fast enough that we're under capacity no matter how well we schedule. There's also a people dimension: reclaiming idle allocations will be mildly annoying for the people who've grown used to treating reserved GPUs as personal property, and we should handle that with communication rather than surprise enforcement. If the six-week experiment turns into a political fight, that's a signal to stop and buy.

But on the evidence we have, the cheapest, most reversible, and most informative next step is to fix how we use what we own — and to pre-commit, in writing, to buying more if the numbers say we still need it. I'd like agreement on the time-box and the trigger by end of next week, so we can start the scheduler work the following Monday.

Happy to walk anyone through the utilisation data in detail before we decide.

**MEMO**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Thursday

We've reached the point in the quarter where the queue for our inference cluster is visibly backing up, and the question on the table is whether we should buy more hardware or get more out of the hardware we already own. I want to lay out my thinking on this before our planning session on Monday, because I don't think the answer is as obvious as the backlog makes it look.

The case for buying is straightforward and emotionally compelling. Our utilization dashboards show peak-hour saturation, jobs are queuing, and researchers are losing afternoons to waiting. Every week of delay has a real opportunity cost: experiments that don't run are experiments whose results we don't have, and in a competitive environment that's a cost that never shows up on an invoice. Hardware lead times are also long, so if we're going to buy, the argument goes, we should buy now. I take all of that seriously.

But when I look at the actual numbers, the picture gets more complicated. Our fleet-level utilization sits around 45 percent averaged across the day, even though peak demand pushes individual nodes past 90 percent. That gap is the tell. We don't have a capacity problem so much as a scheduling and fragmentation problem: large jobs grab whole nodes, small jobs can't pack into the leftovers, overnight capacity goes unused, and nobody owns the queue. Buying more hardware in this state would be like adding lanes to a road with a broken traffic light. It would help for a while, and then we'd be back in the same position, having spent capital to postpone a fix we'll need anyway.

The economics also favor the cheaper path first. Improving utilization — better bin-packing of workloads, a proper job scheduler, time-shifting batch work into the overnight trough, and consolidating the small models currently squatting on big cards — costs us mostly engineering time, maybe two to three weeks of focused effort from one or two people. Buying equivalent capacity outright would cost tens of thousands of dollars up front, plus ongoing power, cooling, and maintenance, and it would arrive months from now. There's also a hidden cost in the purchase option that's easy to miss: hardware depreciates fast, and if our workload mix shifts — which it has twice this year already — capacity we buy for today's shapes may not fit tomorrow's. Utilization improvements, by contrast, are largely reversible and portable. If we tune the scheduler and it turns out we were wrong about demand, we've lost a few weeks of one engineer's time. If we buy and we were wrong, we're holding depreciating silicon.

Reliability cuts both ways, and I want to be honest about that. Right now, our peak-hour saturation means we have no headroom: when a node fails, queued jobs back up dramatically and recovery is slow. More hardware would genuinely improve fault tolerance. But so would better utilization, indirectly — a well-packed cluster with a managed queue degrades more gracefully than a saturated one, because there's slack to absorb failures and requeue work. And the act of building proper scheduling and monitoring makes our operational posture better regardless of what we decide about hardware later.

So my recommendation is this: spend the next three to four weeks on utilization, with a specific, measurable target — fleet utilization above 70 percent and median queue wait under 30 minutes — and treat the purchase decision as deferred, not cancelled. If we hit those targets and demand keeps growing, we buy, and we'll buy with much better information about what we actually need: how many nodes, of what size, for which workload shapes. If we miss the targets, that failure itself will tell us something important about whether our demand is real or whether it's an artifact of inefficiency.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. Utilization projects have a way of expanding, and there's a risk we spend a month optimizing and still end up needing hardware, in which case we'll have traded a month of delay for information. I think that trade is worth it — the information alone justifies it — but I don't want to pretend the delay is free. If someone on the team believes the backlog is already costing us more than a month of opportunity, I want to hear that argument on Monday, with numbers.

One concrete guardrail: if median queue wait exceeds two hours for two consecutive weeks during the optimization window, we escalate the purchase decision immediately rather than letting the project drift. That keeps us honest in both directions.

My default is that we optimize first and buy second, and I'd like to walk into Monday aligned on that, or with a strong counterargument on the table.
